item.title: Bill Simmons’s Podcast Co-Hosts Are Tired of His A.I. Antics
item.description:
Bill Simmons, the iconoclastic podcaster and sports columnist, often uses his airtime to dissect the foibles of well-known figures such as Roger Goodell, the commissioner of the National Football League, and Prince Harry and Meghan, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

But this week the online ire is focused on Mr. Simmons.

Film buffs are complaining about several instances in which Mr. Simmons used ChatGPT — which he sometimes accidentally mispronounces “ChatGBT” — to approximate the opinions of the deceased film critic Roger Ebert in his movie podcast, “The Rewatchables.” Some argued that it was disrespectful of Mr. Ebert; others said it was incongruous that Mr. Simmons, a columnist, would use technology to misappropriate another writer’s work.

Ads from OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, have run on the show this year.

Mr. Simmons’s frequent co-host on “The Rewatchables,” Sean Fennessey, inflamed the controversy on Sunday when he publicly criticized that use of A.I. alongside another colleague, Amanda Dobbins. All three work for The Ringer, the media company and podcast network that Mr. Simmons founded in 2016 and is now owned by Spotify.

In an interview on the podcast “Talk Easy,” Sam Fragoso, its host, asked Mr. Fennessey and Ms. Dobbins whether they had a “moral issue” with the use of A.I. to channel Mr. Ebert now that OpenAI was a sponsor.

“We’ve said, ‘Eh, that’s not cool,’” Mr. Fennessey responded, referring to himself and Chris Ryan, another frequent co-host.

In a reaction video that was widely shared online, Ms. Dobbins looked surprised that OpenAI was a sponsor. “Oh, brother,” she said. “OK, well, I didn’t know that.”

Mr. Simmons, Mr. Fennessey and Ms. Dobbins did not respond to requests for comment.

The episode is the latest backlash to artificial intelligence, from concerns about the data centers that power the technology to questions about job displacement and the ownership of creative work. (The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied the suit’s claims.)

Some of Mr. Simmons closest observers have for months criticized his use of A.I. to conjure Mr. Ebert’s opinions, at least on chat threads dedicated to The Ringer and its podcasters. In March — the last time Mr. Simmons used A.I. to invoke Mr. Ebert from beyond the grave on “The Rewatchables” — Mr. Simmons’s co-hosts pushed back against the segment.

“Roger Ebert sadly passed away in 2013,” Mr. Simmons began.

“You going to disgrace yourself by asking ChatGPT?” Mr. Ryan chimed in.

“I did,” Mr. Simmons said, eliciting laughter and a groan from his co-hosts. “ChatGBT said, ‘Probably three and a half stars.’” The A.I. app said Mr. Ebert “had a strong appreciation for great comedic performances,” Mr. Simmons said.

On an episode in July, Mr. Simmons said he wasn’t including an A.I.-generated “review” from Mr. Ebert because Mr. Ryan had told him not to do it anymore.

During his interview with Mr. Fragoso, Mr. Fennessey also described tension created by Spotify’s decision to license shows created by The Ringer to Netflix.

“There’s an inherent conflict with the work that we’re doing,” Mr. Fennessey said. He added, “I don’t think it totally makes sense for a show that’s covering films released by Netflix to be licensed nonexclusively to Netflix.”

A spokeswoman from Spotify said The Ringer maintained creative control over its programming.

Mr. Simmons hasn’t directly addressed this week’s online uproar over his use of A.I. But on Tuesday, he addressed a different hot-button issue that also has brought him scrutiny. This weekend, Mr. Simmons revealed that he had asked his daughter’s boyfriend to place wagers on his behalf on FanDuel in Massachusetts. Betting through proxies is illegal in Massachusetts, and the state’s gaming commission said it was looking into his remarks.

In a preface to his podcast on Tuesday, Mr. Simmons expressed contrition.

“I learned my lesson — apparently, proxy betting not allowed,” he said. “I actually thought it was, but that’s fine. And now my daughter has to break up with her boyfriend. That was the other thing that they ruled. No, I’m kidding. They’re going to stay together. But I did learn.”

item.title: Get to Know Your Phone’s Built-In Emergency Kit
item.description:
Simple voice calls have long been useful for getting help in a crisis, but today’s smartphones can do so much more. Many can even automatically contact emergency services if you’re incapacitated.

Your phone can give warnings for dangerous situations like storms, floods, wildfires and earthquakes. And if you’re stranded out of network range, many newer devices can connect to a satellite for requesting assistance. Here’s an overview.

First, take time to explore your phone’s settings and menus. Find the places to list emergency contacts, your medical information, permission to share your location and other vital details that can get aid to you faster.

Android has a Safety & Emergency menu in the main settings, and Google includes a Personal Safety app with Android. Samsung’s website has a guide for its Android-based Galaxy phones.

The iPhone’s settings offer a variety of personal safety tools like Emergency SOS and Medical ID. (Apple’s website hosts a 178-page PDF guide to it all.)

Most weather apps will warn you of storms, floods, tornadoes and other dangers. But make sure you’ve turned on the app’s notifications in the settings.

Without a weather app, your phone can still receive wireless emergency alerts sent by government agencies like the National Weather Service.

To see your phone’s wireless emergency alert controls, open the main settings app. On most Android devices, scroll to Safety & Emergency and tap Wireless Emergency Alerts. On an iPhone, tap Notifications and scroll down to the Government Alerts section.

Even if it’s just a few seconds of notice, a warning that an earthquake is about to hit can give you time to find cover. Both Android and iOS include earthquake warnings for light shaking — or for a more serious quake. (Alerts may not be available in all areas, and some earthquakes may go undetected.)

In California, Oregon and Washington, Google has teamed up with the U.S. Geological Survey and its ShakeAlert earthquake early warning system to bring the alerts to Android-based phones (including Samsung Galaxy models).

Elsewhere, the Android Earthquake Alert System turns the more than two billion Android phones out there into pocket seismometers by crowdsourcing and analyzing accelerometer data from the devices. Go to Settings to Safety & Emergency and tap Earthquake Alerts to check the setting and to see a demo.

On an iPhone, tap Settings, select Notifications and scroll down to Enhanced Safety Alerts. Tap it to see the toggles for Earthquake Alerts and Imminent Threat Alerts (for sudden storms, active shooters and other dangers).

For Pacific coastal states, the Seismology Lab at the University of California, Berkeley, offers the free MyShake app for early warnings.

Thanks to the accelerometer and other components, your phone may be able to detect a serious car accident — and automatically dial 911 with your location information if you are incapacitated.

If your Android phone supports this feature, you should see a Car Crash Detection option in the Safety & Emergency menu in the phone’s settings. Many Google Pixel phones offer it.

The feature is included on iPhone 14 models running iOS 16 and later. You can find it by going to Settings, selecting Emergency SOS and looking under Crash Detection.

Most phones offer a silent shortcut for calling emergency services during a crisis, usually by pressing the power button five times or holding down a side button. Look for the Emergency SOS menu in the settings to configure it on an iPhone, Pixel, Motorola or Galaxy device.

No network signal? If you’re outdoors with a clear view of the sky, a satellite connection might come to the rescue. The SOS service was originally free for the first two years of new phone ownership. Apple and Google have extended the offer for an extra year, but expect a notice when things change. (Some wireless carriers, including Verizon and T-Mobile, also have general satellite options with certain plans, or charge an extra $10 a month with others.)

Google has included Satellite SOS to get help by text message on its recent Pixels. You can set it up and see a demo by going to Settings to Safety & Emergency and tapping Pixel Satellite SOS. Samsung has also been adding the satellite option to certain Galaxy phones.

Apple added the Emergency SOS via satellite option with the iPhone 14. If nothing works when you try to call or text 911, the iPhone will try to connect you to a satellite for help by text.

You can try a demonstration of the experience by going to Settings to Emergency SOS to Emergency SOS via Satellite and tapping Try Demo. (Apple has a Roadside Assistance satellite text service for stranded drivers and nonemergency text by satellite, too.)

Exploring these tools for physical safety may not be the most exciting part of phone ownership. But in an unpredictable world, it’s good to know they’re there before you need them.

item.title: Saturday Evening Post Will Stop Printing After 205 Years
item.description:
For more than two centuries, The Saturday Evening Post has chronicled American life in its pages, enshrining a homespun national identity and printing some of the nation’s greatest writers.

That’s changing next year.

The magazine’s January issue will be its last in print, according to Joan SerVaas, the president and publisher. In a letter to The Post’s 50,000 subscribers in the most recent issue, she attributed the decision to a combination of “rising production costs, declining advertising revenue and shifting reader habits.”

“We’ve been dealing with it for over a decade,” Ms. SerVaas said in an interview. “We continued hoping it would turn around or life would get better. Now we’re pretty sure it’s not going to get any better.”

The magazine, which debuted in 1821, will continue to publish new articles and fiction online.

Ms. SerVaas said she had decided to end the print edition because it was a financial drain on the Saturday Evening Post Society, which owns The Post. The archives, which will be preserved online, contain news articles as well as poetry, fiction and art, including iconic images by Norman Rockwell.

The decision was painful for Ms. SerVaas, 72, whose father rescued The Post from financial ruin half a century ago. In 1969, the magazine stopped publishing after poor management decisions and fighting among shareholders left it destitute. Beurt SerVaas, a Midwestern millionaire, amassed a sizable stake in 1970 with his wife, Cory SerVaas, and sharply winnowed the magazine’s debt along with its staff.

Cory SerVaas, a journalist and a physician, revamped The Post, adding coverage on health and wellness issues. Imagining her parents’ reaction to her decision to discontinue the print edition, Joan SerVaas said, “I think about my mother a lot, because she would kill me. She would not be happy, but she would understand.”

Though many magazines have been depleted by the nosedive in print advertising, The Post has fallen from particularly stratospheric heights.

Its largest issue, a 272-page doorstop that published months after the 1929 stock market crash, weighed almost two pounds, according to a 1985 case study from Harvard Business Review. That issue alone generated $1.5 million — the equivalent of $29.2 million today — from 214 national advertisers, and required six million pounds of paper and 120,000 pounds of ink. Sixty 45-ton presses churned it out over three weeks.

In 1903, Jack London was serializing “The Call of the Wild” in its pages. Mary Roberts Rinehart covered World War I from the trenches. In the 1960s, Pete Hamill, a legendary New York journalist, chronicled Hollywood’s new era for The Post. Swaths of Joan Didion’s groundbreaking book “Slouching Towards Bethlehem” were first published by The Post.

There were also some low points. In 1942, a three-part series on Jewish Americans concluded with an article titled, “The Case Against the Jew,” resulting in the cancellation of subscriptions. The magazine apologized.

In 1967, a landmark lawsuit against The Post by Wally Butts, a former athletic director for the University of Georgia, helped solidify legal protections against libel even though the magazine lost the case.

The next year, in a business maneuver inconceivable by today’s standards, The Post cut its own subscription list in half, part of a bid to reach a more selective audience for upscale advertisers.

Ms. SerVaas has focused on digitizing the archives. In 2018, she and her team rolled out a new website that allowed readers to trawl half a million pages and roughly 3,500 covers. She remains hopeful that a new buyer might want to resurrect The Post, the way her family did decades ago.

“I want the best for the magazine,” Ms. SerVaas said. “I want it to continue.”

item.title: FiveThirtyEight’s Podcast Hosts Reunite for a New Show
item.description:
FiveThirtyEight, the politics site and podcast known for deep dives on statistical predictions, was shuttered last year after a series of layoffs and strategy shifts by its corporate owner.

Now, the people behind its popular flagship podcast — Nate Silver, Clare Malone and Galen Druke — are betting they can resurrect its spirit with a new show called “Still Counting.”

The three hosts want the podcast to be just as nonpartisan and empirical as its forebear, as they cover the 2026 midterm elections and new topics like the role of artificial intelligence and prediction markets in politics.

But they’re starting over under the umbrella of an unabashedly progressive media company started by three Obama administration veterans, Crooked Media. FiveThirtyEight was previously licensed or owned by major traditional media brands including The New York Times, ESPN and ABC News.

They say they are confident the show will work even under the new owners.

“There is a market for people who think politics is important, are intellectually interested in it and think it’s high stakes, but don’t want things filtered through a partisan lens,” Mr. Silver said. “That’s one of our markets.”

And they are hoping that their audience, built up over years, will follow them to the new venture, in the latest test of whether the star power in journalism now lies more with individual personalities or with the institutions they worked for.

Lucinda Treat, the chief executive of Crooked Media, said the company had been looking to expand into coverage of artificial intelligence and prediction markets before connecting with “Still Counting.” She said that despite the company’s progressive bona fides — its flagship show is “Pod Save America” — she wanted to ensure the new hosts felt comfortable to do a nonpartisan show.

“We are very focused on fact-based critical information and actionable knowledge,” she said.

Mr. Silver started FiveThirtyEight as a blog in 2008. It skyrocketed in popularity in the lead-up to that year’s presidential election, when Mr. Silver correctly predicted the presidential election winner in 49 states.

After a series of ownership transfers, FiveThirtyEight landed at ABC News, which is owned by Disney. By early 2025, Disney shut down the site and laid off the remaining staff members as part of broader cuts. In May, ABC News removed the archived version of the website from the internet.

Mr. Silver, who left FiveThirtyEight in 2023, said his recent success with his Substack, Silver Bulletin, which has more than 320,000 subscribers, had shown him that FiveThirtyEight could have succeeded in the new media environment if Disney had worked out how to monetize it.

A Disney representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Silver, Ms. Malone and Mr. Druke, who met working at FiveThirtyEight, together hosted the “FiveThirtyEight Politics” podcast from 2016 through 2020.

Last year, they began experimenting with live shows, hosting half a dozen at New York’s Comedy Cellar venue. The events sold out, a sign to them that there was still an audience for their kind of data-focused analysis with a side of banter, especially heading into a midterm election and the 2028 presidential primaries.

“There is an election nerd community out there that has been following a lot of our work even since we’ve let FiveThirtyEight that’s been rooting for a reunion,” Mr. Druke said.

“Still Counting” will come out weekly, with an introductory episode on Wednesday and the first full episode releasing next Wednesday. The show will focus on data analysis and polling while also delving into the new worlds of A.I. and betting markets, “the big existential questions of politics,” Ms. Malone said.

Mr. Druke acknowledged that there was much more skepticism around data and polling now than a decade ago. “Being a savvy observer of politics and data means not resigning oneself to this idea that all polling is wrong,” he said. “It’s being smart enough to know the caveats to append.”

All three hosts will continue their day jobs. Mr. Silver writes his Substack newsletter about politics, sports and artificial intelligence. Ms. Malone, a media and politics writer for The New Yorker, is on leave to write a book about the Make America Healthy Again movement. Mr. Druke hosts “GD Politics,” a podcast and newsletter.

item.title: What Rising Global Bond Rates Mean for Your Money
item.description:
“Soaring” global bond yields. Global bond “sell-offs.”

Headlines in recent days have included many scary words. But what do they mean for you and your money?

As ever, the answer is this: It depends.

It depends on whether you own bonds, what bonds you own and how soon you may need the money you invested. Many people who invest through popular funds in their workplace retirement accounts may know little about their bond holdings, even if they remember that they have roughly 30 percent of their money in bonds.

The good news is that for now, the tumult in the bond markets has not caused big losses in most people’s portfolios. Still, a bit more vigilance is wise at a time like this. In fact, it can be reassuring.

Here are some questions worth asking.

When an investment appears increasingly risky, investors demand to be paid more to take on that risk — and right now, that’s essentially what’s happening in the government bond market.

Though the bond market has been increasingly volatile in recent months, investors around the world sold off government bonds at a faster clip on Tuesday, which caused prices to drop and pushed bond yields, along with interest rates, to recent highs.

Investors are worried about a variety of risks: mounting government debt levels, the U.S.-led war in Iran and its effect on oil prices and inflation, and the heavy borrowing and spending on artificial intelligence.

Rising interest rates on government bonds influence consumer rates on mortgages, student loans, credit cards and more. (The yield on 10-year U.S. Treasury notes, arguably the world’s most instrumental interest rate, reached its highest point since January 2025, while the 30-year yield remained near a two-decade high.)

But the bond market makes up a sizable part of many investors’ portfolios. Bond fluctuations also have implications for the average worker and retiree — higher interest rates, on the whole, help buoy savings over the long run, but it’s complicated (we’ll get into that in a minute).

Let’s say you put money away for a retirement in a target-date fund, an investment vehicle that is named for the year you hope to stop working. Those funds have a mix of stock, bond and sometimes other funds.

Your job is to figure out which underlying bond funds the bond portion of your savings is in. Then, once you have those names, you can look up those funds and see what and how they’re doing.

If you’re in the Vanguard Target Retirement 2040 Fund, your bond investments will be in a U.S. bond fund and a separate international one. Both of them have positive returns over the past year because they invest in all sorts of bonds aside from those government ones. So no big losses to see here.

If a financial adviser has bought bond funds for you — or individual bonds — ask for an accounting and an explanation of the strategy.

Bonds are for diversification, balance and stability, and they’ve historically provided it more often than not.

The bond market includes corporate, municipal and other bonds besides the government ones that have been in the headlines recently. Bonds have had lower returns than stocks over time, but they also lack the volatility of stocks.

Think about it this way: When you’re investing in bonds, you’re lending money with the expectation that the borrowing government, town or company that has issued the bonds will pay you back in full. Most often, that actually happens, plus you collect a bit of interest income along the way to account for the risk of nonrepayment.

And when you hear about “yields rising,” it can mean that’s a decent time to be a lender through bonds.

“Income itself is a really powerful diversifier,” said Matt Wrzesniewsky, head of fixed income client portfolio management at Vanguard. That’s true especially right now, he said, when so many high-quality bonds offer yields above 5 percent.

Do you have investments that you’ve chosen based on your net worth, health, risk tolerance and any people or cause you want to support? If so, nothing is happening right now that should cause you to make big changes.

This may be a good opportunity to rebalance, though. Stocks have had a good run recently, and if you intend to have 60 percent of your portfolio there and 40 percent in bonds, that run-up in stocks may have put you near 70 percent. So you could sell some stock and buy some shares in a bond index fund that will contain those high-quality bonds.

For more on investing in bonds, read our colleague Jeff Sommer’s deep dive on the topic from August.

At their core, bonds are debt instruments: When a government, a city or a company wants to raise cash, it can issue bonds. It pays its lenders (investors) a fixed interest rate over a specific term. The longer the term to maturity (or when the lender is repaid), the higher the rate borrowers will generally pay. In the U.S. government bond market, short-term debt obligations are called Treasury “bills,” medium-term are Treasury “notes” and longer-term instruments are “bonds.”

Longer-term bonds also tend to be more sensitive to interest rate fluctuations than shorter-term bonds. You can get a sense of how your bond fund’s value will react to interest rate changes by looking at its “duration,” measured in years, with longer-duration funds being more sensitive.

The broad Vanguard Total Bond Market Index fund has a duration of 5.5 years, while the Vanguard Long-Term Bond Index fund has a duration of 12.7 years. Generally speaking, for every percentage point that interest rates rise, a bond fund’s value will decline by its duration (the opposite is also true if rates decline). But since bond funds also pay its investors income, the overall drop would not be as steep.

Who knows? The reckoning question is a serious one, and this is actually a serious nonrhetorical question sitting in as an answer.

Logic dictates that governments can’t spend more than they take in and pay for it by borrowing forever. But it would be foolish to bet a chunk of your life savings on the forecaster who attempts to predict when and how the reckoning will come — and what sort of investment to make to profit from it.

So, again, who knows? Very few people, if any.

Here’s one observation that may be helpful even if it isn’t reassuring: We Americans don’t tax ourselves enough to pay for all of the promises the government has made and the expenses in the federal budget. We’ll probably see less generous benefits, lower spending or higher taxes — or all three — within the next decade or two.

You probably won’t be sorry if you’re able to save a bit more with that outcome in mind.

item.title: Employer Health Costs Are Expected to Spike in 2027
item.description:
Large and small employers are bracing for what looks to be the sharpest increase in health care costs in more than two decades. The cost per worker is projected to go up an average of 11 percent next year, or somewhat lower if workers’ insurance benefits are reduced, according to a U.S. survey released Wednesday.

Note: Increase amounts assume no changes to plans and are for employers with 50 or more employees.

Source: Marsh.

By The New York Times

The employers’ final costs, after they make changes to health plans, are still expected to increase about 8 percent next year, the steepest since 2003, according to Marsh, the benefits consultant formerly known as Mercer.

More than a third of the 1,800 employers surveyed said they anticipated that costs would rise at least 10 percent after making cuts.

“This year was a rough year, and next year looks like it will be even rougher,” said Beth Umland, director of employer research for health and benefits at Marsh, in an interview.

The Marsh survey is the latest report by an employer group or benefit consultant predicting a sharp rise in health care costs next year. Many Americans, even those with insurance, are already struggling to afford care, according to various surveys, and health care has become a top issue for voters.

“This seems to be a new normal,” said Ellen Kelsay, the chief executive of Business Group on Health, which represents large employers that offer health benefits.

From 2018 to 2027, health care costs could increase 76 percent, roughly twice the rate of general inflation, according to a survey the employer group released last month. For next year, companies predicted a 9.2 percent median increase, which fell to 8 percent after they made benefit changes.

The cost of providing coverage to employees is becoming an existential business issue, said Mike Pasterick, an executive at the insurance broker Aon, which issued its own projection last month. Aon estimated employers’ costs would rise 9.5 percent next year, pushing the average cost per employee above $19,000 if no changes are made. “This is impacting the companies in a very material way,” he said.

The upshot is that about 160 million people under 65 who rely on employers for health insurance will again confront higher costs and shoulder more of the burden. More and more, workers are facing year-over-year increases that further stress household budgets already dealing with the growing expenses of groceries and gasoline.

Workers are facing higher premiums, deductibles and co-pays, which require them to carry a larger share of their medical bills. Some companies are cutting benefits by discontinuing coverage of expensive GLP-1 drugs to treat obesity, or dropping coverage for spouses who have other insurance options.

Employers and benefits consultants cited a number of factors contributing to higher costs: rising prices for hospital care and prescription drugs, including expensive medicines for cancer, and robust demand for GLP-1 drugs to treat conditions like diabetes.

But they also pointed to new contributors like hospitals’ and doctors’ use of artificial intelligence to increase payments through better documentation of care. They also blamed increasing reimbursements to some doctors who are out of network and are exploiting a new consumer protection law that allows them to challenge what they were originally paid.

The pressure by hospitals and doctors to charge employers even more is likely to intensify with looming cuts to government plans like Medicaid, the federal-state program for low-income individuals. Hospital groups are already seeing an increase in the number of patients who don’t have insurance or can’t pay their bills, and many are expected to charge employers more to help make up for lost revenue.

Many employees are already being asked to pay significantly more of their medical bills. Workers are paying an average of 10 percent more in out-of-pocket costs in 2026 — some $2,167 — than they were last year, Aon estimated.

These kinds of increases are not sustainable, said Rosa Novo, the benefits administrator for Miami-Dade County Public Schools, which covers about 45,000 employees and their families. “It’s become really, really difficult, extremely difficult,” she said. The bulk of the system’s costs are for hospital care, she said, but among the fastest-growing expenses are pharmacy costs.

For the first time, the school system is exploring new ways of delivering care. “We’re having to reinvent the way we operate,” Ms. Novo said. The system is considering contracting directly with hospitals and doctors for some of its employees’ care, like imaging, rather than relying on its insurer to negotiate for it. The system is also starting to demand more visibility into what it pays for care, requiring audits and detailed information about claims.

“I personally see a readiness to do things differently,” said Elizabeth Mitchell, the chief executive of the Purchaser Business Group on Health, which represents employers. She said employers were more interested in seeing more information from insurers about how they were spending their money and consideration of alternatives.

“It’s more than just talk,” she said, saying many companies are revisiting their arrangements with their insurer or pharmacy benefit manager.

Like the Miami-Dade school system, many companies are in discussions directly with local hospital groups or other organization to provide care outside their traditional insurance plans. Others are contemplating ways to steer patients to select hospitals or doctors, either by charging them less to see those providers or limiting where employees can get care.

“We’re seeing a lot of employers taking a closer look at the network,” said Eric Miller, a vice president at Segal, another benefits consultant, despite concerns that employees will be upset if they can’t see their longtime doctor or go to the hospital of their choice.

“Unequivocally, there is more openness to change and disruption than there ever has been,” he said.

Smaller employers may be making the most significant changes, said Shawn Gremminger, the chief executive of the National Alliance of Healthcare Purchaser Coalitions, many of whose members are smaller companies.

“I think it’s the smaller market where the pain is most acute,” he said.

While some are considering moves like offering employees a fixed amount of money to pay for a plan, others are taking a close look at the giant companies that sell them insurance or pharmacy benefit management. In the alliance’s most recent survey, 54 percent of employers said they were working with one of the three largest pharmacy benefit managers, a drop from 63 percent the year before. Many said they were moving to one of the smaller pharmacy benefit managers, many of which promise more transparency about how they operate and what they pay for drugs.

“We may be seeing a tipping point,” Mr. Gremminger said.

item.title: Markets Waver as Investors Assess War, Debt and Inflation
item.description:
Investors on Wednesday weighed the aftermath of another wave of strikes across the Middle East, as U.S. forces hit military targets in Iran and Iran retaliated against American bases in Jordan and Iraq. Commercial ships in the Persian Gulf have also come under attack.

The surge in violence in recent days, after a month without U.S. strikes, has pushed oil prices back above $90 a barrel. In turn, the higher cost of energy is feeding through to more expensive gasoline, diesel and other refined fuels. And fears of accelerating inflation have bucked financial markets, especially bonds, compounding worries about debt levels and deficits. Rising borrowing costs also threaten to squeeze consumers and businesses, a risk to economic growth and a relatively resilient stock market.

The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, traded at just under $95 a barrel, flat on the day. But the price began the week below $90 and is now up more than 30 percent since the start of the war.

West Texas Intermediate crude, the U.S. benchmark, was about $90 per barrel.

Investors and analysts are focused on the continued disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that before the war carried as much as one-fifth of the world’s oil supply and a large amount of gas. The Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen have also restricted tanker traffic in the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, which Saudi Arabia has used as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.

How much the international benchmark costs

Notes: Data shows future contract prices for Brent crude oil. Gaps indicate nontrading hours. Data is delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

Shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz remained slow, with only six ships transiting on Tuesday, according to Kpler, a maritime data company. Many vessels are traveling in the region with their navigation devices turned off to evade detection, making them difficult to track. Before the war, more than 130 ships a day transited the strait.

Navigating the region’s waterways remains a dangerous endeavor. On Monday, two oil tankers were attacked while passing through the strait. No fatalities were reported from the strikes. At least 19 commercial seafarers have been killed in the Middle East since the war in Iran began, according to data from the International Maritime Organization.

U.S. forces, which are blockading Iranian oil at sea from exiting the region, are helping ships navigate the southern route near Oman. Iran has taken near total control of deciding which ships pass through the strait close to its coastline.

Note: Data may not include all activity because some vessels have turned off tracking capabilities.

Source: Kpler.

Jason Karaian/The New York Times

The national average price of gasoline went up two cents on Wednesday to $4.12 a gallon, according to the AAA motor club. The price has risen 39 percent since the war began.

Gas prices don’t move in lock step with crude, usually trailing increases or declines by a few days.

The average price of diesel jumped six cents on Wednesday to $5.69 per gallon. It is up 51 percent since the start of the war. On Tuesday, President Trump hosted a group of oil company executives at the White House, as he pushes the industry to expand refinery capacity in an effort to bring down prices.

Here is a county-level look at where drivers are facing the highest costs.

S&P 500 futures pointed to a slight decline when trading resumes in the United States on Monday. The index is on a three-day losing streak.

In Europe, the Stoxx 600, a broad index that tracks the region’s largest companies, dipped 0.6 percent.

Stocks in Asia fell. The Nikkei 225, the benchmark index in Japan, dropped 2.9 percent and the KOSPI in South tumbled 4 percent. Stocks in China ended lower.

How stocks are trading in the United States

Note: Data delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

Government bonds appeared shaky again on Wednesday, the day after a global sell-off put investors on edge. Unease among bond buyers has been building, driven by government deficit and debt levels, the Iran war’s effect on inflation and heavy borrowing by tech companies building out artificial intelligence systems.

U.S. Treasury yields, which measure government borrowing and influence interest rates on mortgages and business loans, remain elevated. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note hovered around 4.8 percent, the highest in more than a year.

Japan’s 10-year government yield pushed further above 3 percent, the highest since the mid-1990s. Government yields across Europe also continued to rise, with bonds issued by Britain, France and Germany creeping up to fresh highs not seen in a decade or more.

item.title: Chevron Expansion in Venezuela Extends U.S. Influence Over Oil Riches
item.description:
Chevron plans to significantly expand its operations in Venezuela, the U.S. oil giant said on Wednesday, taking yet another step to broaden the U.S. sphere of influence in the South American country.

The Houston-based company, already Venezuela’s largest private oil producer, said it would more than double its production in the country over the next five years to 600,000 barrels a day. That represents over half of Venezuela’s current output.

Chevron, which is gaining access to new areas in the oil-rich Orinoco Belt region, plans to invest more than $7 billion in Venezuela in that period.

The company announced its plans days after President Trump said his administration was pursuing a highly unusual partnership with a different oil company that would give the U.S. government a direct hand in extracting oil on foreign soil.

The two deals are separate, but both advance Mr. Trump’s goal of exerting much more control over Venezuela’s energy industry after U.S. forces captured the country’s leader, Nicolás Maduro, in January.

“Our expanded position reflects our confidence in the country’s deep resource potential and its ability to compete for investment within our portfolio for decades,” Chevron’s chief executive, Mike Wirth, said in a statement.

A signing ceremony is scheduled for later on Wednesday at the presidential palace in Caracas. Mr. Maduro’s successor, Delcy Rodríguez, and the U.S. energy secretary, Chris Wright, are expected to attend.

Under pressure from the Trump administration, Venezuela has been making changes to attract American companies and other foreign investors roughly two decades after the country nationalized the oil industry. In January, the country’s National Assembly voted to give foreign companies much greater control over their Venezuelan operations.

Chevron, in turn, has been steadily expanding in the Orinoco Belt, including by agreeing earlier this year to trade assets with Venezuela’s state-owned oil company, Petróleos de Venezuela.

As of earlier this summer, Chevron was producing around 280,000 barrels of oil a day in Venezuela and expected to increase that by up to 50 percent by the end of 2028, said Eimear Bonner, the company’s chief financial officer. That output is shared with the Venezuelan state oil company, its partner there.

Chevron pumps around 4 million barrels of oil and natural gas a day globally at an estimated cost of more than $18 billion in capital spending this year.

Chevron is unique among big American oil producers for remaining in Venezuela after the country forced foreign companies to accept smaller stakes in their projects when it nationalized the industry. Exxon Mobil and ConocoPhillips left after refusing to accept those changes.

Chevron’s decision to stay — which looked at times like a very bad bet — now appears to be paying off. The company has been in a prime position as the Trump administration has sought to carve out a bigger role for U.S. companies in Venezuela.

That said, the Trump administration’s new partnership, which is with an influential and divisive Venezuelan businessman, Alejandro Betancourt López, may complicate Chevron’s standing in the country by elevating a competitor. Mr. Betancourt’s family controls Venezuela’s second-largest private oil producer, North American Blue Energy Partners.

Under the deal announced by the administration, the U.S. government would receive the option to acquire an ownership stake of 35 percent in the parent company of North American Blue Energy Partners. The United States would also secure preferential access to the oil that the company produced and considerable say over its corporate governance.
